sections.h2: How does a residential eviction work in Mississippi?
sections.html:
A landlord must give written notice, file a sworn affidavit or complaint in court, win a judgment, and then have the sheriff or a constable carry out a warrant of removal. The rules for homes and apartments sit in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Title 89, Chapter 8 of the Mississippi Code.

That chapter was rewritten in 2022 and amended again in 2025, so older summaries can be out of date. Section 89-8-31 says a landlord may start eviction proceedings for breach of the rental agreement or for failing to vacate after the agreement ends. Nothing in the chapter lets an owner skip the court step.

The older Chapter 7 sections, including 89-7-27, apply to premises that are not a dwelling unit, such as commercial space. If you own a rented house, Chapter 8 is the one that governs.

sections.h2: What notice does a Mississippi landlord have to give?
sections.html:
The notice period depends on why the tenancy is ending. Notice must be in writing, and email or text counts only if the tenant agreed in writing to be notified that way.

SituationNotice requiredStatute
Unpaid rentWritten notice that the agreement ends if rent is not paid within 3 days89-8-13(5)
Other material breach by tenantTermination date not less than 14 days after receipt, if not fixed within a reasonable time up to 14 days89-8-13(3)
Month-to-month tenancy30 days written notice89-8-19(3)
Week-to-week tenancy7 days written notice89-8-19(2)
Substantial violation affecting health or safetyNo notice required89-8-19(4)

A breach that can be repaired is treated differently. Under Section 89-8-13, if the tenant fixes the problem before the date in the notice, the rental agreement does not end. If substantially the same breach comes back within six months, the landlord may terminate on at least 14 days of notice.

Unless a lease sets a fixed term, tenancy is week to week for tenants who pay weekly and month to month in every other case. A landlord who sells to a buyer wanting the house vacant often ends up using the month-to-month notice.

sections.h2: What does a landlord file to start the case?
sections.html:
The landlord files a sworn affidavit or complaint and a copy of the notice that was delivered. Section 89-8-33 says the affidavit must state the facts requiring removal and identify the dwelling address and any rent or fees owed.

After filing, the court issues a summons. Section 89-8-35 requires the summons to tell the tenant that the judge will decide whether the landlord is entitled to possession, that a tenant who loses has at least seven days from the judgment to move out unless the judge sets a different period, and that a tenant sued for nonpayment can stop the eviction by paying everything owed. Service follows the Mississippi Rules of Court.

sections.h2: How long does the hearing take and what can the judge order?
sections.html:
The statute puts a hard outer limit on the hearing. Section 89-8-41 allows either side to ask for an adjournment, but a single adjournment cannot exceed ten days unless both parties consent, and no adjournment can push the entire hearing past 30 days from the date the case was filed.

Other points the statute sets out:

  • The court must grant a default judgment if the landlord filed the required papers, the summons was properly served, and the tenant did not appear (89-8-37).
  • Judgments must be signed and executed on the same business day they are granted.
  • If the landlord wins, the judge orders the tenant to vacate within seven days unless an emergency or other compelling circumstance justifies a shorter or longer period (89-8-39).
  • A shorter period can be justified when the tenant committed a substantial health or safety violation or poses an immediate risk of damage or injury.

Check the current text of the statute and confirm timing with the court clerk in the county where the house is, since the chapter was amended in 2022 and again in 2025.

sections.h2: What happens after the move-out date passes?
sections.html:
Only law enforcement can remove a tenant, and only under a warrant. After the court-ordered move-out date the landlord may request a warrant of removal, and on payment of fees the judge issues it to the sheriff or a constable of the county.

The statute adds details that matter to owners. A warrant is not executed when it is simply posted on the door. Officers must remove the occupants and put the landlord in physical possession. For 72 hours afterward the landlord must give the tenant reasonable access to collect belongings. After that, remaining property may be moved to the curb or another agreed location.

In a case based only on unpaid rent, Section 89-8-39 bars the warrant if the tenant has paid in full all unpaid rent and other sums awarded by the move-out date, and it obliges the landlord to accept that payment in good faith. Appeals follow the Mississippi Rules of Court under 89-8-43.

sections.h2: How does an eviction affect selling a rented house in Mississippi?
sections.html:
It affects timing, cost, and what condition the house is in when you hand it over. A landlord who wants to sell has three realistic paths, and each one has a different clock.

  • Give a notice to end the tenancy, then sell once the house is vacant.
  • File for eviction because of unpaid rent or a breach, then sell after possession is returned.
  • Sell the house with the tenant in place and let the buyer deal with the lease.

Read the lease before choosing the third path. This guide cannot confirm a statewide rule for how an existing lease binds a new owner, so have an attorney or the title company review it. Do not shut off utilities, change locks, or remove belongings to force a move. The statute routes possession through a court judgment and a warrant.

A cash buyer can buy a rented house as-is, including one that needs repairs after a difficult tenancy. The sale does not remove any court deadline that has already started, and nobody should promise you a closing date until the possession question is clear.

sections.h2: How do property tax classes change when a house is a rental?
sections.html:
A rented single-family house is taxed differently from the owner's own home. The Department of Revenue defines Class I as single-family, owner-occupied residential real property assessed at 10 percent of true value, and Class II as all other real property at 15 percent.

Homestead exemption also requires that the applicant own and occupy the home as a primary residence on January 1. A landlord who moves out and rents the house generally cannot keep claiming it. The assessor makes the final call, so ask the county Tax Assessor if you are unsure.

Property tax is due by February 1 for the preceding assessment year, and an unpaid balance can lead to the county tax sale. Check for a delinquent balance before you list a rental, especially if the tenant stopped paying and the house sat in dispute for months.

faqs.q: How many days notice is needed to evict for unpaid rent in Mississippi?
faqs.a: Three days. Under Section 89-8-13(5) the landlord delivers written notice that the rental agreement will end if rent is not paid within three days. Email or text works only if the tenant agreed in writing.

faqs.q: How long does a Mississippi eviction take?
faqs.a: The hearing cannot be adjourned beyond 30 days from the filing date under Section 89-8-41, and a tenant who loses generally gets seven days to move out. Total time also depends on notice, service, and how soon the sheriff or constable acts on the warrant.

faqs.q: Can a landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?
faqs.a: No. The statute provides a court judgment and a warrant of removal served by the sheriff or a constable. A warrant posted on the door is not executed, and officers must physically put the landlord in possession.

faqs.q: Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying?
faqs.a: In a nonpayment case, yes. Section 89-8-39 says the judge shall not issue a warrant if the tenant paid all unpaid rent and other sums awarded by the court-ordered move-out date, and the landlord must accept that payment in good faith.

faqs.q: Do different rules apply to commercial tenants?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 89-7-27 covers premises that are not a dwelling unit and allows removal after default in rent and three days of written notice, among other grounds. Residential cases use Chapter 8.
